cards.explanation: The answer is the altar. Jeroboam, king of Israel, is standing beside it to burn incense when the man of God calls out, “O altar, O altar, this is what the LORD says…” (1 Kings 13:2). The message is aimed at the altar, and the king is right beside it.

The sign is that the altar will split apart. The man of God says, “Surely the altar will be split apart, and the ashes upon it will be poured out.” A sign is something you can check with your own eyes. Jeroboam doesn't have to take anybody's word for it.

The king's hand withers and gets stuck. Jeroboam stretches out his hand and says, “Seize him!” But the hand he stretched out "…withered, so that he could not pull it back." He orders a man seized and can't even take his own hand back. I think that's a long moment to stand there holding a pose you didn't choose.

The answer is pray. Jeroboam says, “Intercede with the LORD your God and pray for me that my hand may be restored.” The man he wanted seized is now the man he's asking for help. The text gives us what the king asks, and it doesn't say what was going on inside him.

The answer is False. The man of God turns the king's offer down flat. The text has him say, “If you were to give me half your possessions, I still would not go with you, nor would I eat bread or drink water in this place.” A king's reward and a seat at his table, and the answer is no. Even I would have to think twice about that one.

The reason is that the LORD commanded him not to. The man of God says it himself: “For this is what I was commanded by the word of the LORD: ‘You must not eat bread or drink water or return by the way you came.’…” It's a command from the LORD. That's why a king's reward can't move him.

The answer is that he takes a different road. The text says he "…went another way and did not return by the way he had come to Bethel." The command had three parts, and he follows the road part as well. So far he's sticking to every piece of it.

The old prophet asks his sons which way the man went. His question is, “Which way did he go?” and they show him the road the man of God took. Short question, friends, but watch what it sets in motion. Next thing you know, he's telling his sons to saddle the donkey (1 Kings 13:12, 13). I think somebody just made up his mind.

The answer is False. The man of God says no to the old prophet's invitation. He answers, “I cannot go home with you, and I will not eat bread or drink water with you in this place.” Then he explains that the LORD told him, “You must not eat bread or drink water there or return by the way you came.” So the old prophet's invitation gets turned down.

The answer is True. The text says so outright: "The old prophet was lying to him…" He says, “I too am a prophet like you, and an angel spoke to me by the word of the LORD…” but the man of God had already been told something different by the word of the LORD. We're told this plainly so we know the angel claim wasn't true.

The man of God goes back and eats at the old prophet's house. The text says he "…went back with him, ate bread in his house, and drank water." He had told the king and then the old prophet he wouldn't. Now he does the very thing he said he wouldn't do.

The word of the LORD comes to the old prophet. The text says, "…the word of the LORD came to the prophet who had brought him back…" It comes while they're sitting at the table. The old prophet is the one who tells the man of God what it says.

The answer is defied. Here's the message: “Because you have defied the word of the LORD and have not kept the commandment that the LORD your God gave you…” Defied is a strong word, and the LORD chose it. It names what happened at that table.

The men passing by report it in the old prophet's city. They see the body and the lion beside it, and they go and report it in the city where the old prophet lived. The text doesn't say what they did beyond that.

The answer is False. The old prophet doesn't call it chance. He says, “It is the man of God who disobeyed the command of the LORD.” Then he adds that the LORD has delivered him to the lion according to the word the LORD had spoken to him. It's a heavy moment, and the old prophet treats it that way.

The answer is True. The text says, "The lion had not eaten the body or mauled the donkey." The old prophet finds the body with the donkey and the lion standing beside it. I think that's a strange scene to ride up on, and the text lets it speak for itself.

He lays the body in his own tomb. He lifts it onto the donkey and brings it back to his own city to mourn and bury him. Earlier the LORD's message said the man's body would never reach the tomb of his fathers (1 Kings 13:22). The text just tells us where he's laid.

The answer is bones. The old prophet tells his sons, “When I die, you must bury me in the tomb where the man of God is buried. Lay my bones beside his bones…” He's thinking ahead to his own burial. He gives his reason too: the message the man of God cried out against the altar “…will surely come to pass.”

The reason is that the man's message will surely come true. The old prophet says it right after the burial: “…for the message that he cried out by the word of the LORD against the altar in Bethel and against all the shrines on the high places in the cities of Samaria will surely come to pass.” That's the reason the text gives. It names the message the man of God cried out.

Jeroboam makes anyone who wants it a priest. The text says "…again he appointed priests for the high places from every class of people. He ordained anyone who desired to be a priest of the high places." The word again tells us he's done this before. After all that happened, he keeps going.

The answer is True. The text says it plainly: “…this was the sin of the house of Jeroboam that led to its extermination and destruction from the face of the earth.” That sin is Jeroboam appointing priests for the high places. It's a heavy way to end the passage, and the text doesn't soften it.
